title: Sums of Two Squares
short: n is a sum of two squares exactly when every prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) appears in its factorization to an even power.
trouble: Students rule out every n with a prime factor that is 3 mod 4, but 45 = 3² · 5 = 6² + 3².

blocks.html: $5 = 1^{2} + 2^{2}$ and $13 = 2^{2} + 3^{2}$, but no matter how you try, $7$ and $21$ are not sums of two squares. Fermat found the pattern, and the supplementary law for $-1$ is the key to it.

Theorem (Fermat; proved by Euler). An odd prime $p$ is a sum of two squares exactly when $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. More generally, a positive integer $n$ is a sum of two squares of integers exactly when every prime $q \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ appears in the prime factorization of $n$ to an even power.

Why $3 \bmod 4$ primes fail. Squares are $0$ or $1 \bmod 4$, so a sum of two squares is $0$, $1$ or $2 \bmod 4$, never $3$.
Products of sums are sums. $(a^{2} + b^{2})(c^{2} + d^{2}) = (ac - bd)^{2} + (ad + bc)^{2}$, an identity you can check by expanding.
Primes $\equiv 1 \bmod 4$ succeed. Here $-1$ is a square mod $p$: some $x$ has $p \mid x^{2} + 1$, a sum of two squares divisible by $p$. A short argument (Thue's lemma, or Fermat's "descent") shrinks this to $p$ itself.
Why even powers. If $q \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ divides $a^{2} + b^{2}$, then $q$ divides both $a$ and $b$ (otherwise $-1 \equiv (a b^{-1})^{2}$ would be a square mod $q$). So $q^{2}$ divides the sum, and dividing it out leaves a smaller sum of two squares.

blocks.title: Primes
blocks.q: Write $13$ and $29$ as sums of two squares, and explain why $23$ cannot be one.
steps: $23 \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, and a sum of two squares is never $3 \bmod 4$.

blocks.title: A prime 3 mod 4, squared
blocks.q: Is $45$ a sum of two squares?
steps: $45 = 3^{2} \cdot 5$: the prime $3 \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ appears to an even power, so yes.

blocks.title: Multiplying representations
blocks.q: Write $65 = 5 \cdot 13$ as a sum of two squares in two ways.
steps: Swapping the roles of $c$ and $d$ gives $(4 - 3)^{2} + (6 + 2)^{2} = 1 + 64$.

blocks.html: Ruling out every number with a prime factor that is $3 \bmod 4$. $45 = 3^{2} \cdot 5$ has the factor 3, yet $45 = 6^{2} + 3^{2}$: the 3 appears squared. Only an odd power of such a prime is fatal, as in $21 = 3 \cdot 7$ or $63 = 3^{2} \cdot 7$. Also remember that $0$ counts: $49 = 7^{2} + 0^{2}$.
$n$ is a sum of two squares exactly when each prime $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ divides $n$ to an even power. Primes $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ are sums of two squares, and products of sums are sums.
